It’s a question many have been asking after a FlyDubai plane headed for Israel made a harrowing emergency landing after one pilot stabbed the other in the cockpit. Our reporters in Tel Aviv, Dubai and London bring you new details and passenger accounts of the fight to subdue the attacker and regain control of the plane. In this video , aviation reporter Benjamin Katz analyzes the flight’s extreme descent rate, tracking data and rare security implications. Much about the episode remains unclear. But the near-disaster has sent a shudder through a region racked by three years of war, and raised a host of troubling possibilities that officials are just beginning to investigate.

READ IT HERE FIRST   Money managers are asking clients to give the bond market another chance.   Wealth advisers and investment managers are trying to convince their clients to embrace an asset class that many have grown to despise. They want investors to get back into bonds to take advantage of tempting yields. But it’s a tall task after years of topsy-turvy returns. And it’s only got harder with benchmark yields at the highest level in two-dozen years, and prices inversely falling. At the heart of the pitch is that bonds are doing what they are supposed to be doing, by at least one measure for the first time in years, report Oyin Adedoyin and Miriam Gottfried.

   5.   Google pushed AI into schools—and teachers and students say learning suffered.   No tech giant has been more aggressive in putting AI in front of schoolchildren than Google. The company’s ubiquitous presence in American classrooms through Chromebooks and software partnerships has provided a critical launchpad for its AI tools to reach kids. But the rollout has helped push many students to become academically and emotionally dependent on AI, according to interviews with more than 60 teachers, school officials, parents, children and clinicians. Google’s own researchers have written that the technology can pose elevated risks to children, and has potential for cognitive and emotional harm, report Shalini Ramachandran, Georgia Wells and Molly Reinmann. 1. FROM MY DESK

 

What happened on Flight 1073? It’s a question many have been asking after a FlyDubai plane headed for Israel made a harrowing emergency landing after one pilot stabbed the other in the cockpit. Our reporters in Tel Aviv, Dubai and London bring you new details and passenger accounts of the fight to subdue the attacker and regain control of the plane. • Senate Democrats are challenging the legality and prudence of the Pentagon’s plan to take a stake in a Venezuelan oil company.

 

• Just over two months into his tenure as U.K. prime minister, Andy Burnham is laying the groundwork for an unabashedly socialist overhaul of the British state.

 

• A new drone command, a ban on “ideological clowns,” a study on future war tech—and more. Here are five takeaways from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s speech.

 

• A U.S. pressure campaign has left dozens of Iranian tankers stranded in Asian waters as Washington threatens sanctions against anyone coming to their assistance.

• Investors are betting big on Grail’s Galleri multi-cancer test. But the Medicare money the business depends on is far from guaranteed, writes David Wainer.

 
 
 

4. READ IT HERE FIRST

 

Money managers are asking clients to give the bond market another chance.

 

Wealth advisers and investment managers are trying to convince their clients to embrace an asset class that many have grown to despise. They want investors to get back into bonds to take advantage of tempting yields. But it’s a tall task after years of topsy-turvy returns. And it’s only got harder with benchmark yields at the highest level in two-dozen years, and prices inversely falling. At the heart of the pitch is that bonds are doing what they are supposed to be doing, by at least one measure for the first time in years, report Oyin Adedoyin and Miriam Gottfried.

 

5.

 

Google pushed AI into schools—and teachers and students say learning suffered.

 

No tech giant has been more aggressive in putting AI in front of schoolchildren than Google. The company’s ubiquitous presence in American classrooms through Chromebooks and software partnerships has provided a critical launchpad for its AI tools to reach kids. But the rollout has helped push many students to become academically and emotionally dependent on AI, according to interviews with more than 60 teachers, school officials, parents, children and clinicians. Google’s own researchers have written that the technology can pose elevated risks to children, and has potential for cognitive and emotional harm, report Shalini Ramachandran, Georgia Wells and Molly Reinmann. A Google spokeswoman said that studies show that AI tools paired with teacher-led instruction can help students learn more effectively.

6. SEE THE STORY

 

All this man thinks about is what he can shrink next. It made him a toy tycoon.

 
 
TONJE THILESEN FOR WSJ
 

Most entrepreneurs dream big. Alan Dorfman does the opposite. He spends every waking hour trying to shrink things to their smallest possible size without losing their functionality. Dorfman has churned out miniature versions of thousands of products including the Rubik’s Cube, the Operation board game and Hungry Hungry Hippos. In a world of endless entertainment options, somehow there’s growing demand for impossibly tiny toys. Dorfman says Americans’ enduring appetite for novelty has got stronger recently as people seek out the low-tech thrills of earlier eras.

8. THE NUMBER

 
>5.3%
 

The 10-year Treasury yield climbed above 5.3% on Wednesday, blowing past its 2007 peak to reach its highest level since 2002. The milestone is particularly notable because it hints that U.S. borrowing conditions haven’t just returned to a pre-2008-09 financial crisis normalcy, as some investors have recently suggested. Instead, something even bigger might be afoot.

 
 
 

9. AND FINALLY…

 

Your grip strength can tell you a lot about your health.

 

What’s in a forearm? Turns out, a lot. Grip strength is increasingly being viewed as an important biomarker of our overall strength and fitness. Even in children, studies have found grip strength to be associated with cardiometabolic health. A weak grip is associated with a higher risk of heart disease, Type 2 diabetes, osteoporosis, stroke and dementia.
